extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, tragedians, and students of literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative principles for composing poetry and especially tragedy: how to choose subjects, construct plots, portray character, and use diction, song, and spectacle to produce the tragic effect (pity and fear) and catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as the defining principle of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry (and certain musical arts) are modes of imitation (mimesis): they represent actions, characters, and life rather than merely reporting facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand poetic production as imitation: the poet is an imitator or 'maker' whose work produces universals (what may happen) rather than particulars (what has happened). This principle underpins all other evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Different arts differ by their medium: rhythm, language, and 'harmony' (music) are used singly or in combination to imitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate medium(s) for your genre: flute/lyre use harmony and rhythm; dancing uses rhythm; some poetic forms use language alone (prose or verse); tragedy and comedy employ combinations including song, diction, and spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects imitated are men in action, portrayed as better, worse, or as they are; comedy tends to represent men as worse, tragedy as better than in real life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your work aims to elevate, debase, or present life truthfully; this choice determines tone and moral stance—tragedy prefers elevated types, comedy the lower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation (narration vs dramatic presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may imitate by narration (telling) or by presenting characters as living and moving before the audience (dramatic representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatic presentation for action-based forms (drama), and use narration where appropriate (epic, historical epic); be aware that the choice affects audience engagement and the means of producing pity/fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished by rhythm, harmony, and song; in the form of action, not narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition as the checklist for tragic quality: seriousness, completeness, magnitude, appropriate language/embellishment, enactment of action, and capacity to produce catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy must have six parts which determine its quality: Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or design a tragedy by attending to each part; priority is given (see separate entries) but all six contribute to overall effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (the soul of tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the arrangement of incidents—the imitation of action—and is the first and most important principle of tragedy; the end (purpose) of the play is chiefly in the incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plots where incidents are artistically ordered; a play may lack character and yet be tragic if the plot is well-built. Ensure peripeteia and recognition emerge from plot structure rather than contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be a whole (beginning, middle, end) and of proper magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole has a beginning (which does not follow anything by necessity), a middle, and an end (which follows something but is followed by nothing). Magnitude must allow the sequence of events to be grasped and produce change (good↔bad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arbitrary starts/ends; choose a length the audience/memory can embrace. Order parts so that removing any part disturbs the whole—every scene should be organically necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (structural unity, not unity of hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot is the imitation of one action; it does not mean recounting every incident in one person's life. The parts must be structurally united such that removal of any part disjoints the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center the drama on a single coherent action with causal/probable links among incidents. Do not confuse a single protagonist's many adventures with a single dramatic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events must follow probability or necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must relate what may happen according to the law of probability or necessity; incidents should be causally or probabilistically connected, not mere coincidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build causal chains or convincing probability; avoid implausible coincidences unless they have the air of intentional design and arise from prior incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epeisodic plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: An epeisodic plot is one in which episodes succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence; such plots are the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not string together striking episodes for display; aim instead for organic continuity where each episode grows naturally from the preceding ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex plots preferred (use of reversal and recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex plots incorporate Reversal (peripeteia) and/or Recognition (anagnorisis), producing a change of fortune through internal plot logic; these are superior to simple plots where change occurs without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for reversals and recognitions that arise necessarily or probably from prior incidents, heightening pity and fear and producing a more powerful tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change by which the action veers round to its opposite, governed by probability or necessity (e.g., a messenger sent to relieve becomes the cause of despair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft reversals that are surprising yet logically/rhetorically necessitated by the plot; they should turn expectation into its opposite and be rooted in prior events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change from ignorance to knowledge producing love or hate between persons; best when coincident with reversal, especially recognition of identity or deed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognition scenes to reveal previously unknown ties or facts in a way that redefines actions and produces emotional impact; recognition ideally emerges from plot mechanics, not forced exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene of suffering (pathos)
rubrics_metrics.description: A destructive or painful action such as death on stage, bodily agony, wounds, etc., which is a constituent of the plot producing tragic feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include suffering when it grows from the plot and deepens pity/fear; avoid gratuitous horror that shocks without tragic consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of protagonist (character leading to pity and fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist should be neither eminently good nor entirely villainous but of a mixed character: renowned and prosperous, whose downfall is due not to vice but to some error or frailty (hamartia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select heroes whose high status makes their misfortune moving, and whose error (not moral depravity) plausibly causes reversal—this arouses pity and fear in the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character qualities (four aims: goodness, propriety, likeness to life, consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character should (1) be good (manifest moral purpose), (2) show propriety (appropriate traits for sex/status), (3) be true to life (credible), and (4) be consistent (if inconsistent, consistently so).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test each character against these four points; avoid motiveless degradation, inappropriate traits, implausible behavior, or erratic inconsistency that breaks verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (intellectual element / reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances—where something is proved, or a general maxim enunciated; it discloses the speaker's reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make speeches and reasoning appropriate to situation and character; thought supplies the logical or philosophical weight of the play and should support actions and recognitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (language, metrical arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of meaning in words and the metrical arrangement; it is essential in both verse and prose and must be clear and apt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diction to express character and thought; balance elevation with perspicuity (poetic diction should combine loftiness and clarity). Avoid obscure or decoratively grotesque language that undermines understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction / appropriate language
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic diction must unite elevation (the poetic tone) with perspicuity; metaphors and stylistic devices are fitting but should not obscure the sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ poetic devices where they illuminate truth or character; prioritize intelligibility so that the audience can feel pity and fear from the incidents themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song (musical element) as chief embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Song (choral odes, lyrical elements) is the principal embellishment of tragedy and occupies a chief place among decorative parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate song where it naturally arises from the action and contributes to mood, thematic reinforcement, or pacing; it should be harnessed to the plot's emotional trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (stagecraft) is least artistic but emotionally potent
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (scenic display) has emotional attraction but is least connected with poetic art and depends more on stagecraft than on the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on internal plot structure first to produce tragic effect; use spectacle as supplement, not as substitute for effective plotting and character work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of familial or close relations to arouse pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic incidents are most moving when they occur between persons who are near or dear (brother/father/son/mother etc.), since such ties intensify pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, root tragic reversals and recognitions in intimate relationships or kinship ties to maximize emotional stakes; handle traditional legends skillfully but feel free to invent plausible variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper outcome and single issue
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed tragedy should have a single issue (not double) and typically a change from good fortune to bad (not vice versa); the downfall should arise from error, not vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a unified catastrophe rather than dual threads leading to opposite resolutions. Avoid uplifting endings for tragedy that undermine tragic pleasure; double-thread plots may cater to weak spectators but dilute true tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative/structural parts (prologue, episode, exode, parode, stasimon, commos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into quantitative parts: Prologue (before first choral entry), Episode (between choric songs), Exode (final part with no choric song after), Parode (first utterance of Chorus), Stasimon (choral ode without marching metres), and Commos (joint lament).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize a play with attention to these divisions; use choric parts to reflect on and amplify the action, and episodes to carry forward the plot. Know the formal function of each part when structuring scenes and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form choice: Epic vs Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and Tragedy share many elements (both imitate noble actions) but differ: Epic uses one metre (hexameter) and is narrative with no strict time limit; Tragedy is enacted, uses varied forms of language/song, and aims at a single revolution of the sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose form according to scale and mode of presentation: use epic for wide-ranging narrative and Tragedy for concentrated enacted action; recognize that mastery of tragic elements also informs epic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry aims at the universal (not mere history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry expresses the universal—what types of persons will do under certain conditions—whereas history reports particulars that have happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In composing, aim to depict general truths about human action and character through particular incidents; avoid slavish adherence to historical particulars that do not serve universal insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid producing terror/monstrosity merely by spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacle, but superior poetry produces these emotions from the internal structure of the piece; reliance on spectacle to create mere horror is inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize plot-driven emotional effects. Use spectacle sparingly and only where it serves the plot and deepens tragic emotion rather than merely startling or repelling the audience.
